content: 1. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has provided technical guidance on applying a human rights-based approach to implementing policies and programs aimed at reducing preventable maternal morbidity and mortality. This guidance was presented during the 20th session of the Human Rights Council in 2012 in New York. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations for the induction of labor, including specific guidelines for induction at or beyond term. These recommendations were published in Geneva in 2018 and are accessible through the WHO IRIS platform. 3. A Cochrane systematic review by Kelly AJ, Alfirevic Z, and Ghosh A compared outpatient versus inpatient induction of labor to improve birth outcomes. The findings are available in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 4. Reid M, Lorimer K, Norman JE, Bollapragada SS, and Norrie J explored the appropriateness of home settings for cervical ripening prior to labor induction. Their study, published in Midwifery in 2011, highlights the potential benefits of home-based care for certain women. 5. The GRADE approach, a widely used framework for grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in healthcare, is detailed in the Handbook for Grading the Quality of Evidence and the Strength of Recommendations, edited by Schünemann H, Brożek J, Guyatt G, and Oxman A. The handbook was last updated in October 2013. 6. Balshem H, Helfand M, Schünemann HJ, Oxman AD, Kunz R, Brożek J, et al. provided detailed guidelines on rating the quality of evidence in their publication in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2011. 7. Rehfuss EA, Stratil JM, Scheel IB, Portela A, Norris SL, and Baltussen R emphasized the integration of WHO norms and values with a complexity perspective in their 2019 article in BMJ Global Health. 8. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition) outlines the processes for creating evidence-based recommendations. This document is available on the WHO IRIS platform. 9. Vogel J, Dowswell T, Lewin S, Bonet M, Hampson L, Kellie F, et al. described the development and application of a living guidelines approach for WHO recommendations on maternal and perinatal health in their 2019 publication in BMJ Global Health. 10. Alfirevic Z, Gyte GML, Nogueira Pileggi V, Plachcinski R, Osoti AO, and Finucane EM conducted a Cochrane review comparing home versus inpatient induction of labor to improve birth outcomes. The review was published in 2020. 11. The WHO's 2015 report, State of Inequality: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health, provides a comprehensive analysis of health disparities and is accessible through the WHO data platform. 12. Tong A, Flemming K, McInnes E, Oliver S, and Craig J developed the ENTREQ framework to enhance transparency in reporting qualitative research synthesis. Their work was published in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2012. 13. Adeslson PL, Wedlock GR, Wilkinson CS, Howard K, Bryce RL, and Turnbull DA conducted a cost analysis comparing inpatient and outpatient prostaglandin E2 cervical priming for labor induction. The results, derived from the OPRA trial, were published in Australian Health Review in 2013. 14. Wilkinson C, Adeslson P, and Turnbull D compared inpatient and outpatient balloon catheter cervical ripening in a pilot randomized controlled trial. Their findings were published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth in 2015. 15. The WHO's 2018 joint statement, developed in collaboration with UNFPA, UNICEF, ICM, ICN, FIGO, and IPA, defines skilled health personnel providing care during childbirth. This document is available on the WHO IRIS platform. 16. Vogel JP, Gülmezoglu AM, Hofmeyr GJ, and Temmerman M discussed global perspectives on elective labor induction in their 2014 article in Clinical Obstetrics and Gynecology. 17. Vogel JP, Souza JP, and Gülmezoglu AM analyzed patterns and outcomes of labor induction in Africa and Asia using data from the WHO Global Survey on Maternal and Neonatal Health. Their findings were published in PLOS One in 2013. 18. The WHO's recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience include updates on maternal and fetal assessment, such as imaging ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy. These guidelines are accessible through the WHO IRIS platform. 19. Standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities are outlined in a WHO publication available on the WHO IRIS platform. 20. Coates R, Cupples G, Scamell A, and McCourt C conducted a qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis of women's experiences with labor induction. Their findings were published in Midwifery in 2019. 21. Akuamoah-Boateng J and Spencer R reviewed women's experiences and perceptions of labor induction for uncomplicated post-term pregnancy. Their systematic review of qualitative evidence was published in Midwifery in 2018. 22. Lou S, Hvidman L, Uldbjerg N, Neumann L, Jensen TF, Haben JG, et al. conducted a systematic review of qualitative studies on women's experiences with post-term labor induction. Their findings were published in Birth in 2019. 23. Coates D, Goodfellow A, and Sinclair L explored the experiences of care and decision-making among women and clinicians during labor induction. Their study was published in 2020. 24. Henderson J and Redshaw M conducted a mixed-methods study on women's experiences with labor induction, published in Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica in 2013. 25. Wessberg A, Lundgren I, and Elden H conducted a phenomenological study on women's lived experiences of pregnancy at 41 weeks and beyond. Their findings were published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth in 2017. 26. Nippita TA, Porter M, Seeho SK, Morris JM, and Roberts CL examined variations in clinical decision-making for labor induction in a qualitative study published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth in 2017. 27. The WHO Steering Group, along with various experts and contributors, developed recommendations on outpatient settings for labor induction. These guidelines are supported by evidence synthesis and external reviews, ensuring a robust and transparent development process. 28. Outcomes related to labor induction were ranked on a scale of 1 to 9, with scores of 7 or higher considered critical and scores of 4–6 deemed important. Critical maternal outcomes include failure to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours, cesarean section, uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes, postpartum hemorrhage, uterine rupture, and severe maternal morbidity or death. 29. The WHO's recommendations on outpatient settings for labor induction are supported by a comprehensive review of evidence and expert input, ensuring alignment with global health priorities and standards.
